nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; short-story writer, novelist and editor writing in English
literary_identity: American short-story writer and collagist, the most inventive practitioner of American postmodern fiction, whose hundred-odd stories in The New Yorker remade the short story as a structure of jokes, quotations and interruptions
biography: Donald Barthelme Jr. was born in Philadelphia on 7 April 1931, the son of an architect, and grew up in Houston, Texas, where his father taught at the University of Houston. He studied journalism there, wrote for the Houston Post, founded and edited the literary magazine Forum, was drafted into the army in 1953 and served in Korea as editor of an army newspaper, and in 1961 became director of the Contemporary Arts Museum in Houston, the year he published his first story. He was managing editor of Location and a co-founder of Fiction, and from 1963 The New Yorker published more than a hundred of his stories. Come Back, Dr. Caligari (1964) collected the first of them; Snow White (1967), first serialised in The New Yorker, was his first novel, followed by Unspeakable Practices, Unnatural Acts (1968), City Life (1970), the children's book The Slightly Irregular Fire Engine (1971, National Book Award 1972), Sadness (1972), Guilty Pleasures (1974), The Dead Father (1975), Amateurs (1976), Great Days (1979), Sixty Stories (1981), Overnight to Many Distant Cities (1983), Paradise (1986), Forty Stories (1987) and The King (1990, posthumous). He taught at Boston University, the University at Buffalo and the City College of New York, where he was distinguished visiting professor in 1974-75, and died of throat cancer in Houston on 23 July 1989.
literary_profile: Stories: Come Back, Dr. Caligari (1964), Unspeakable Practices, Unnatural Acts (1968), City Life (1970), Sadness (1972), Amateurs (1976), Great Days (1979), Sixty Stories (1981), Overnight to Many Distant Cities (1983), Forty Stories (1987), Flying to America (2008) and Collected Stories (2021). Novels: Snow White (1967), The Dead Father (1975), Paradise (1986) and The King (1990). Non-fiction and satire: Guilty Pleasures (1974), The Teachings of Don B. (1992) and Not-Knowing (1997). Children's book: The Slightly Irregular Fire Engine (1971).
stylistic_characteristics: Stories without plot in the traditional sense, built by accumulation and juxtaposition; the non-sequitur as a structural device; parody of found forms - the questionnaire, the catalogue, the academic essay, the newspaper column, the interview; dialogue of great flatness and precision; typographic and visual play; a deadpan narrator who reports the absurd as though it were ordinary.
intellectual_concerns: The making of art and the reception of the artwork by a public that wants it explained; the arbitrariness of the signs and objects among which Americans live; marriage, divorce and desire conducted in a language of cliché; the city as a grid and as a joke; death, and the difficulty of saying anything true about it; the exhaustion of inherited literary forms and the freedom that exhaustion offers.
historical_significance: Barthelme is the representative American postmodernist and the writer through whom the American short story after 1965 is usually periodised; his stories are standard anthology and workshop texts, 'The Balloon' and 'The School' are among the most widely reprinted American short stories of the postwar decades, and his influence is acknowledged by writers as different as George Saunders, David Foster Wallace and Lydia Davis. The Library of America collected his stories in 2021, the first such volume for a postwar American experimental short-story writer.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's articles on Barthelme and on his bibliography, read directly, with the first periodical printings of the two Norton selections taken from The New Yorker's own archive and from the bibliography's tables; they were not checked against a printed bibliography. Installment 10 records the two Norton selections - 'The Balloon' (The New Yorker, 16 April 1966; collected 1968) and 'The School' (The New Yorker, 17 June 1974; collected 1976) - so the novels, the other hundred stories and the non-fiction have no records, and the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; poet, novelist and short-story writer writing in English
literary_identity: American poet whose posthumous Ariel (1965) and The Collected Poems (1981) made her the central confessional poet of the postwar period and the most discussed woman poet of the twentieth century
biography: Sylvia Plath was born in the Jamaica Plain district of Boston on 27 October 1932, the daughter of Otto Plath, a German-born professor of biology at Boston University, and Aurelia Schober Plath, a teacher of Austrian descent. Her father died in November 1940, when she was eight, and the grief and anger of that loss became the matter of her best-known poem nineteen years later. She grew up in Wellesley, wrote and published precociously, won a scholarship to Smith College, and in 1953, after a month in New York as a guest editor at Mademoiselle, suffered the first of the breakdowns and suicide attempts that The Bell Jar (1963) describes. She returned to Smith, graduated summa cum laude in 1955, and took a Fulbright to Newnham College, Cambridge, where she met the poet Ted Hughes; they married in June 1956. After two years teaching at Smith she and Hughes moved back to England, and in 1960, after the birth of their daughter Frieda, Heinemann published The Colossus and Other Poems, the only collection of her poetry to appear in her lifetime. In 1961 they settled at Court Green in North Tawton, Devon, where their son Nicholas was born; in the autumn of 1962, after Hughes's affair with Assia Wevill, the marriage broke up and Plath moved with the children to a flat in Fitzroy Road, London. In the last five months of her life she wrote at extraordinary speed - the poems of October and November 1962, including 'Daddy', 'Lady Lazarus', 'Ariel' and 'The Applicant', and the winter poems 'Child' and 'Words' - and in January 1963 published The Bell Jar under the pseudonym Victoria Lucas. She died by suicide in London on 11 February 1963, aged thirty, and is buried at Heptonstall in West Yorkshire. Ariel appeared in 1965 in a text arranged by Hughes, who reordered the manuscript and added poems; Ariel: The Restored Edition (2004) printed her own selection and sequence for the first time. The Collected Poems (1981), also edited by Hughes, won the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry in 1982, the first awarded posthumously to a poet.
literary_profile: Poetry: The Colossus and Other Poems (1960), Ariel (1965), Uncollected Poems (1965), Crossing the Water (1971), Winter Trees (1971), The Collected Poems (1981, Pulitzer Prize 1982), Selected Poems (1985) and Ariel: The Restored Edition (2004). Novel: The Bell Jar (1963, as Victoria Lucas). Prose and letters: Letters Home (1975), Johnny Panic and the Bible of Dreams (1977), The Journals of Sylvia Plath (1982), The Unabridged Journals (2000) and The Letters of Sylvia Plath (2 vols, 2017-2018). Children's books: The Bed Book (1976) and The It-Doesn't-Matter Suit (1996).
stylistic_characteristics: Short stanzas, usually tercets, quintains or loose quatrains, with lines that run over the stanza break and a rhyme that is heard in the vowel rather than at the line end; a diction that moves without warning between the nursery and the clinic, the lyric and the obscene; a first person that is at once exhibitionistic and defensive; repetition and refrain used as a formal device, as in 'Daddy' and 'Lady Lazarus'; the homeliest domestic object - a watch, a shoe, a telephone, a paperweight - made to carry the whole weight of the poem.
intellectual_concerns: The father as the dead origin of speech; the wish to die and the theatrical refusal to stay dead; motherhood, childbirth and the body as the site of another's life; marriage, betrayal and the humiliation of dependence; the Holocaust and the concentration camp as figures for domestic power; the English and American landscape as an image of the mind; the materials of a woman's art - sewing, cooking, beekeeping, riding, drawing - turned into the machinery of vision.
historical_significance: Plath is the poet through whom confessional poetry and the literature of the 1960s are taught, and 'Daddy', 'Lady Lazarus' and 'Ariel' are among the most anthologised and most argued-over poems of the century. Her posthumous reputation - the Pulitzer of 1982, the biographies, the controversy over the editing of Ariel, the part she plays in feminist criticism from the 1970s onward - has made her a case study in the making of a literary reputation as well as a body of work, and her influence on later women poets in English is acknowledged almost everywhere it is discussed.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's articles on Sylvia Plath, on Ariel and on The Colossus and Other Poems, which agree with the contents list of The Collected Poems and with the dates of composition established from the manuscripts at Smith College and printed in the appendix to Ariel: The Restored Edition; they were not checked against a printed bibliography. Installment 10 records the eight Norton selections - 'Morning Song', 'Lady Lazarus', 'Ariel', 'Daddy', 'Words', 'Blackberrying', 'The Applicant' and 'Child' - so the other poems, the novel, the stories, the letters and the journals have no records, and the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; novelist, essayist and editor writing in English
literary_identity: American novelist and the first Black woman to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature (1993), whose eleven novels remade the language of American historical memory and whose editorship at Random House brought Black American writing into the mainstream of trade publishing
biography: Toni Morrison was born Chloe Ardelia Wofford in Lorain, Ohio, on 18 February 1931, the second of four children of a working-class Black family; she took the name Toni at Howard University, where she graduated in English in 1953, and took an MA in American literature at Cornell in 1955 with a thesis on William Faulkner and Virginia Woolf. She taught at Texas Southern University and at Howard, where she met and married the architect Harold Morrison; the marriage ended in 1964, and she moved with her two sons to Syracuse to work as an editor at Random House, where in the late 1960s she became the first Black woman senior editor in the company's fiction department and published Gayl Jones, Toni Cade Bambara, Angela Davis and Muhammad Ali. Her first novel, The Bluest Eye (1970), was written in the early mornings around her editorial work; it was followed by Sula (1973), Song of Solomon (1977), which won the National Book Critics Circle Award, Tar Baby (1981) and Beloved (1987), which won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 1988 and was adapted for film in 1998. She taught at Princeton from 1989 to 2006, held the Robert F. Goheen chair, and wrote Jazz (1992), Paradise (1997), Love (2003), A Mercy (2008) and God Help the Child (2015), as well as Playing in the Dark (1992), The Nobel Lecture in Literature (1994) and the libretto for Richard Danielpour's Margaret Garner (2005). She was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1993, the first Black woman to receive it, and the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2012. She died at Montefiore Medical Center in the Bronx on 5 August 2019.
literary_profile: Novels: The Bluest Eye (1970), Sula (1973), Song of Solomon (1977), Tar Baby (1981), Beloved (1987), Jazz (1992), Paradise (1997), Love (2003), A Mercy (2008) and God Help the Child (2015). Other prose: Playing in the Dark: Whiteness and the Literary Imagination (1992), The Nobel Lecture in Literature, 1993 (1994), What Moves at the Margin: Selected Nonfiction (2008) and The Origin of Others (2017). Children's books, with Slade Morrison: The Big Box (1999), The Book of Mean People (2002) and Peeny Butter Fudge (2003). Drama and libretto: Dreaming Emmett (1986) and Margaret Garner (2005).
stylistic_characteristics: A prose of long, cadenced sentences that move between the vernacular and the biblical; a narrative that withholds its central event and circles it from several voices; the repeated image that returns with a changed meaning; an interior monologue in which memory and present action are not separated; and a refusal of the explanatory paragraph, so that the reader must assemble the history the novel is about.
intellectual_concerns: Slavery and its afterlife in American memory; the construction of race and of whiteness; the mother-child bond under conditions of ownership; the Black community as a source of both shelter and judgement; language as the medium in which the dead and the living speak to one another; music, especially jazz and the blues, as a model of form; and the ethics of remembering what a nation would rather forget.
historical_significance: Morrison is the central American novelist of the last half-century and the one whose work redefined what the American historical novel could do with the enslaved and the dispossessed. Beloved is routinely placed among the finest American novels of the century, the Nobel Prize of 1993 made her the first Black woman to hold it, and her essays on whiteness and on the Africanist presence in American literature have changed the teaching of the subject. Her influence on the generation of Black American writers after 1980 is acknowledged on every side.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's article on Morrison, which agrees with the publisher's and prize records consulted; they were not checked against a printed bibliography. Installment 10 records one Norton selection - the Nobel lecture of 1993 - so the eleven novels, the essays, the children's books and the libretto have no records, and the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; novelist, short-story writer, poet, essayist and critic writing in English
literary_identity: American novelist and man of letters, the most prolific and technically accomplished of the postwar American realists, whose Rabbit tetralogy, Couples and the stories of ordinary Protestant middle life made him the chronicler of the American suburbs and twice won him the Pulitzer Prize
biography: John Hoyer Updike was born in Reading, Pennsylvania, on 18 March 1932 and grew up in the small town of Shillington, the only child of a schoolteacher father and a mother who wrote and painted; the town became the Olinger of his early fiction. He was a brilliant student, edited the Harvard Lampoon, graduated summa cum laude in 1954, and spent a year at the Ruskin School of Drawing in Oxford before joining the staff of The New Yorker in 1955, where he wrote the Talk of the Town column and began publishing the stories and poems that made his name. He left the magazine in 1957 for Ipswich, Massachusetts, where he lived for the rest of his life and wrote, on average, a book a year. The Poorhouse Fair (1959) and Rabbit, Run (1960) were followed by The Centaur (1963, National Book Award), Of the Farm (1965), Couples (1968), Rabbit Redux (1971), A Month of Sundays (1975), The Coup (1978), Rabbit Is Rich (1981, Pulitzer Prize), The Witches of Eastwick (1984), Roger's Version (1986), Rabbit at Rest (1990, Pulitzer Prize), Memories of the Ford Administration (1992), Brazil (1994), In the Beauty of the Lilies (1996), Toward the End of Time (1997), Gertrude and Claudius (2000), Seek My Face (2002), Villages (2004), Terrorist (2006) and The Widows of Eastwick (2008); the stories were collected in The Same Door (1959), Pigeon Feathers (1962), The Music School (1966), Bech: A Book (1970), Problems (1979), Too Far to Go (1979), Bech Is Back (1982), Trust Me (1987), The Afterlife (1994), Bech at Bay (1998), Licks of Love (2000), The Early Stories 1953-1975 (2003) and My Father's Tears (2009). He was a prolific critic and reviewer for The New Yorker and The New York Review of Books, wrote the memoir Self-Consciousness (1989), and died at Danvers, Massachusetts, on 27 January 2009.
literary_profile: Novels: The Poorhouse Fair (1959), Rabbit, Run (1960), The Centaur (1963), Of the Farm (1965), Couples (1968), Rabbit Redux (1971), A Month of Sundays (1975), Marry Me (1976), The Coup (1978), Rabbit Is Rich (1981), The Witches of Eastwick (1984), Roger's Version (1986), S. (1988), Rabbit at Rest (1990), Memories of the Ford Administration (1992), Brazil (1994), In the Beauty of the Lilies (1996), Toward the End of Time (1997), Gertrude and Claudius (2000), Seek My Face (2002), Villages (2004), Terrorist (2006) and The Widows of Eastwick (2008). Stories: The Same Door (1959), Pigeon Feathers (1962), The Music School (1966), Museums and Women (1972), Problems (1979), Trust Me (1987), The Afterlife (1994), Licks of Love (2000), The Early Stories 1953-1975 (2003) and My Father's Tears (2009). Poetry, criticism and memoir: The Carpentered Hen (1958), Assorted Prose (1965), Picked-Up Pieces (1975), Hugging the Shore (1983), Self-Consciousness (1989) and Odd Jobs (1991).
stylistic_characteristics: A precise, sensory prose that gives equal weight to the surface of things and to what they conceal; the present tense used for immediacy, and the long retrospective paragraph for judgement; a narrator who is at once inside a character's consciousness and above it, commenting; a vocabulary drawn from theology, science and the consumer goods of the American century; and a habit of ending a story on a small, unresolved gesture rather than a revelation.
intellectual_concerns: Sexual desire and its consequences in marriage and the suburb; the residue of Calvinism and of Protestant small-town life in the American present; mortality, ageing and the body's decline; the ordinary American century - the Depression, the war, the postwar boom, the 1960s - as it is lived by unremarkable people; the relation of art and faith; and the moral weight of the trivial.
historical_significance: Updike is the most decorated American novelist of his generation - two Pulitzer Prizes, two National Book Awards, three National Book Critics Circle Awards - and the standard chronicler in fiction of the American suburb and of the Protestant middle class in the second half of the twentieth century. The Rabbit novels are a continuous social history of the United States from 1959 to 1989, and his short stories are a standing exhibit in the teaching of the form; his critical essays on American and European writing are a substantial part of his reputation.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's article on Updike, with the contents of Licks of Love taken from a library catalogue record of the Knopf first edition; they were not checked against a printed bibliography. Installment 10 records one Norton selection - 'New York Girl' - so the twenty-four novels, the poems, the criticism and the other stories have no records, and the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; novelist, short-story writer and essayist writing in English
literary_identity: American novelist whose Goodbye, Columbus, Portnoy's Complaint and the Zuckerman and Roth books made the American Jewish family and the American male ego the matter of a fifty-year comic and self-lacerating project
biography: Philip Milton Roth was born in Newark, New Jersey, on 19 March 1933, the second son of first-generation American parents of Galician Jewish descent; the Weequahic neighbourhood in which he grew up became the setting of his first book and of much of his later work. He graduated from Bucknell University in 1954 and took an MA in English at the University of Chicago in 1955, then taught writing at Chicago, Iowa and Princeton while publishing stories in The Paris Review, The New Yorker and Commentary. Goodbye, Columbus (1959), a novella and five stories, won the National Book Award in 1960 and made him, at twenty-six, a controversial figure in the American Jewish community. Letting Go (1962), When She Was Good (1967) and Portnoy's Complaint (1969) followed; the last made him a celebrity and remains one of the most discussed American novels of the period. From the 1970s he wrote the sequence of books narrated by his alter ego Nathan Zuckerman - The Ghost Writer (1979), Zuckerman Unbound (1981), The Anatomy Lesson (1983), The Prague Orgy (1985), The Counterlife (1986), American Pastoral (1997, Pulitzer Prize), I Married a Communist (1998) and The Human Stain (2000) - as well as The Breast (1972), My Life as a Man (1974), Sabbath's Theater (1995, National Book Award), The Dying Animal (2001), The Plot Against America (2004), Everyman (2006), Indignation (2008), The Humbling (2009) and Nemesis (2010). He edited the eight-volume complete edition of his own work for the Library of America, published in the last years of his life, and died in New York on 22 May 2018; he is buried in the Mount Zion cemetery in Queens.
literary_profile: Fiction: Goodbye, Columbus (1959), Letting Go (1962), When She Was Good (1967), Portnoy's Complaint (1969), Our Gang (1971), The Breast (1972), The Great American Novel (1973), My Life as a Man (1974), The Ghost Writer (1979), Zuckerman Unbound (1981), The Anatomy Lesson (1983), The Prague Orgy (1985), The Counterlife (1986), Deception (1990), Operation Shylock (1993), Sabbath's Theater (1995), American Pastoral (1997), I Married a Communist (1998), The Human Stain (2000), The Dying Animal (2001), The Plot Against America (2004), Everyman (2006), Indignation (2008), The Humbling (2009) and Nemesis (2010). Nonfiction: Reading Myself and Others (1975), The Facts (1988), Patrimony (1991) and Why Write? (2017).
stylistic_characteristics: A first-person voice of enormous comic energy that turns on itself, exaggerating its own grievance until the complaint becomes a critique; dialogue recorded with an ear for the exact cliché of its speaker; a narrative that offers several incompatible explanations for the same event and declines to choose; and an insistence on the body, its appetites and humiliations, as the ground of the moral life.
intellectual_concerns: The American Jewish family as the crucible of assimilation and guilt; the sexual life of the American male and its entanglement with vanity and shame; the difference between the story one tells about oneself and the life one has led; Newark and the American city in decline; the political history of the American century, from the Second World War to the Bush years; and the question of what a novelist does with a life that is his own.
historical_significance: Roth is the most awarded American novelist of his generation and, in the judgement of the Library of America, one of the four or five whose work is printed in a complete authorised edition during his lifetime. Goodbye, Columbus is still the standard American story of the child who takes his father's religion more seriously than the adults, and the Zuckerman books and American Pastoral are among the most discussed American novels of the last half-century; his influence on the American autobiographical novel after 1980 is impossible to overstate.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's article on Roth and on Goodbye, Columbus, which give the first printing of 'The Conversion of the Jews' in The Paris Review 18 (Spring 1958); they were not checked against a printed bibliography. Installment 10 records one Norton selection - 'The Conversion of the Jews' - so the thirty-one books and the essays have no records, and the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; novelist and short-story writer writing in English
literary_identity: American science-fiction writer whose novels of unstable reality, simulacra and bureaucratic theocracy - The Man in the High Castle, Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?, Ubik - moved science fiction into the literary mainstream and into the Library of America
biography: Philip Kindred Dick was born in Chicago on 16 December 1928, twin to a sister who died six weeks later, and grew up in Berkeley, California, where his family moved after his parents separated. He attended Berkeley High School and the University of California at Berkeley for a year, worked in a record shop and as a radio announcer, and from 1952 published science fiction at a rate that made him, by the end of the decade, one of the most prolific writers in the field: forty-five novels and one hundred and twenty-one short stories. Solar Lottery (1955) was his first novel; Eye in the Sky (1957), Time Out of Joint (1959), The Man in the High Castle (1962, Hugo Award), Martian Time-Slip (1964), The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch (1965), Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? (1968, the source of Blade Runner), Ubik (1969), Flow My Tears, the Policeman Said (1974) and A Scanner Darkly (1977) followed. From 1974 he experienced the series of visions and voices he called 2-3-74, which he explored in the exegesis published posthumously as The Exegesis of Philip K. Dick (2011) and which informs VALIS (1981), The Divine Invasion (1982) and The Transmigration of Timothy Archer (1982). He died of a stroke in Santa Ana, California, on 2 March 1982, weeks before the release of Blade Runner; the Library of America issued three volumes of his novels between 2007 and 2009, the first science fiction the series had admitted.
literary_profile: Novels: Solar Lottery (1955), Eye in the Sky (1957), The Cosmic Puppets (1957), Time Out of Joint (1959), Dr. Futurity (1960), Vulcan's Hammer (1960), The Man in the High Castle (1962), The Game-Players of Titan (1963), Martian Time-Slip (1964), The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch (1965), Dr. Bloodmoney (1965), Now Wait for Last Year (1966), Counter-Clock World (1967), Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? (1968), Ubik (1969), A Maze of Death (1970), Flow My Tears, the Policeman Said (1974), A Scanner Darkly (1977), VALIS (1981), The Divine Invasion (1982) and The Transmigration of Timothy Archer (1982). Stories: A Handful of Darkness (1955), The Variable Man (1957), The Preserving Machine (1969), The Golden Man (1980), We Can Remember It for You Wholesale (1990) and the five-volume Collected Stories (1987). Nonfiction: The Shifting Realities of Philip K. Dick (1995) and The Exegesis of Philip K. Dick (2011).
stylistic_characteristics: A plain, hurried, colloquial prose that reports metaphysical catastrophe in the tone of a man describing a bad day at work; dialogue full of the slang and the commercial jargon of the American 1960s and 1970s; plots that turn on a single ontological doubt - is this world the real one, and is this self the one that woke up; a cast of small-time entrepreneurs, repairmen, police and addicts; and an ending that refuses the consolation of a solved mystery.
intellectual_concerns: The instability of the perceived world and the possibility that reality is a fabrication or a simulation; the human and the machine, and the point at which a person can no longer tell them apart; entropy, decay and the second law as a moral fact; the theodicy question, asked through cults, gurus and false messiahs; surveillance, bureaucracy and the police state; and addiction, which he wrote about from the inside.
historical_significance: Dick is the most influential science-fiction writer of the postwar period after Asimov and Le Guin, and the one whose work has most thoroughly crossed into the literary canon: the Library of America admitted him in 2007, and the films adapted from his novels and stories - Blade Runner, Total Recall, Minority Report, A Scanner Darkly, The Adjustment Bureau - have made his premises part of the common intellectual furniture of the present. His influence on cyberpunk and on the literary novel of the 2000s is acknowledged by writers as different as William Gibson and Jonathan Lethem.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's bibliography of Dick and from the FictionMags Index, which give 'Precious Artifact' in Galaxy Magazine for October 1964 and its collection in We Can Remember It for You Wholesale (1990); they were not checked against a printed bibliography. Installment 10 records one Norton selection - 'Precious Artifact' - so the forty-five novels and the other hundred and twenty stories have no records, and the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; novelist, short-story writer, poet and essayist writing in English
literary_identity: American writer of speculative fiction and the most decorated author in the field, whose Earthsea books, The Left Hand of Darkness and The Dispossessed made anthropology, gender and anarchist politics the matter of science fiction and brought it into the American literary canon
biography: Ursula Kroeber Le Guin was born in Berkeley, California, on 21 October 1929, the daughter of the anthropologist Alfred Kroeber and the writer Theodora Kroeber, and grew up among the anthropologists and Native American informants who visited her parents' house - an education she later called the source of her interest in invented cultures. She took a BA at Radcliffe in 1951, an MA at Columbia in 1952 with a thesis on the French poet Pierre de Ronsard, and a Fulbright to Paris, where she met the historian Charles Le Guin; they married in 1953 and settled in Portland, Oregon, where she taught French at Portland State University and wrote in the early mornings. Rocannon's World (1966) began the Hainish sequence; A Wizard of Earthsea (1968), The Tombs of Atuan (1970) and The Farthest Shore (1972) made the Earthsea archipelago one of the founding landscapes of modern fantasy; The Left Hand of Darkness (1969) won both the Hugo and the Nebula and is the novel through which the field thinks about gender; The Lathe of Heaven (1971), The Dispossessed (1974), which won the Hugo, the Nebula and the Locus and is the most discussed anarchist novel in English, and The Word for World Is Forest (1976) followed. Always Coming Home (1985) and the later Earthsea books - Tehanu (1990), Tales from Earthsea (2001) and The Other Wind (2001) - deepened the sequence, and her essays in The Language of the Night (1979), Dancing at the Edge of the World (1989) and Words Are My Matter (2016) made her the field's most articulate critic. She was awarded the National Book Foundation's Medal for Distinguished Contribution to American Letters in 2014, and died in Portland on 22 January 2018.
literary_profile: Novels: Rocannon's World (1966), Planet of Exile (1966), City of Illusions (1967), A Wizard of Earthsea (1968), The Left Hand of Darkness (1969), The Tombs of Atuan (1970), The Lathe of Heaven (1971), The Farthest Shore (1972), The Dispossessed (1974), The Word for World Is Forest (1976), Malafrena (1979), The Beginning Place (1980), The Eye of the Heron (1982), Always Coming Home (1985), Tehanu (1990), The Other Wind (2001) and Lavinia (2008). Stories: The Wind's Twelve Quarters (1975), Orsinian Tales (1976), The Compass Rose (1982), Buffalo Gals and Other Animal Presences (1987), A Fisherman of the Inland Sea (1994), Four Ways to Forgiveness (1995), Unlocking the Air (1996) and Changing Planes (2003). Essays and poetry: The Language of the Night (1979), Dancing at the Edge of the World (1989), Steering the Craft (1998), Words Are My Matter (2016) and the collection of poetry Late in the Day (2015).
stylistic_characteristics: A plain, exact and rhythmically poised prose that never strains for effect; invented cultures presented through their own habits, food, kinship terms and proverbs rather than through exposition; a narrator who is a visiting anthropologist or a participant-observer; dialogue that carries the moral argument; and an ending that resolves the plot while leaving the ethical question open.
intellectual_concerns: The anthropologist's question of how a society makes its members - kinship, taboo, gift, ritual; gender and the arbitrariness of the roles attached to it; anarchism, ownership and the possibility of a just political order; death, ageing and the price of immortality; the relation of humans to other species and to the land; and language itself as the technology that makes a world.
historical_significance: Le Guin is the most honoured writer in the history of science fiction and fantasy - six Hugos, six Nebulas, the National Book Award, the PEN/Malamute and a Library of Congress Living Legend award - and the writer who did most to make the field's treatment of gender, politics and anthropology respectable to the literary mainstream. The Left Hand of Darkness and The Dispossessed are set texts in courses on science fiction, on utopia and on feminist theory, and her essays on writing are among the most quoted in the language.
bibliographical_notes: The titles and dates above come from Wikipedia's article on Le Guin, with the first printing of 'Schrodinger's Cat' in Universe 5 (1974), edited by Terry Carr, taken from the anthology's copyright page and from the several accounts of the story's publication; they were not checked against a printed bibliography. Installment 10 records one Norton selection - 'Schrodinger's Cat' - so the twenty-one novels, the other stories and the essays have no records, and the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; novelist and short-story writer writing in English
literary_identity: American science-fiction writer and the first of the field to receive a MacArthur Fellowship, whose Patternist, Xenogenesis and Parable books made race, power and biological necessity the central questions of American speculative fiction
biography: Octavia Estelle Butler was born in Pasadena, California, on 22 June 1947 and was raised by her widowed mother and grandmother; shy, dyslexic and, as she later said, 'a black girl in a white world', she began writing at twelve after seeing the film Devil Girl from Mars and deciding that she could do better. She took an associate's degree at Pasadena City College, attended California State University at Los Angeles and the Clarion Science Fiction Writers' Workshop in 1970, and published Patternmaster (1976), the first of the five Patternist books, which were followed by Mind of My Mind (1977), Survivor (1978), Wild Seed (1980) and Clay's Ark (1984). Kindred (1979), the novel in which a Black woman of 1976 is pulled back to a Maryland plantation to save the life of her white ancestor, made her reputation outside the genre and is now a standard text in American literature courses. The Xenogenesis trilogy - Dawn (1987), Adulthood Rites (1988) and Imago (1989) - was collected as Lilith's Brood; the Parable books, Parable of the Sower (1993) and Parable of the Talents (1998), which won the Nebula, imagined a near-future America of climate collapse and religious fundamentalism. Her stories were collected in Bloodchild and Other Stories (1995) and her journals and essays in Earthseed and elsewhere. She received a MacArthur Fellowship in 1995 - the first given to a science-fiction writer - and the PEN Lifetime Achievement Award in 2000, and died of a stroke in Lake Forest Park, Washington, on 24 February 2006.
literary_profile: Fiction: Patternmaster (1976), Mind of My Mind (1977), Survivor (1978), Kindred (1979), Wild Seed (1980), Clay's Ark (1984), Dawn (1987), Adulthood Rites (1988), Imago (1989), Parable of the Sower (1993) and Parable of the Talents (1998). Stories: Bloodchild and Other Stories (1995, expanded 2005). Nonfiction and journals: Earthseed: The Books of the Living (in the Parable novels) and uncollected essays and interviews. Posthumous: Fledgling (2005) and the unfinished Parable of the Trickster (2020, published in manuscript).
stylistic_characteristics: A plain, declarative prose that reports the most extreme bodily and social situations without raising its voice; a first-person narrator who is usually a survivor and who explains the rules of her world as she learns them; a structural patience that withholds the meaning of an institution until the reader has lived inside it; and a refusal of the villain, since the oppressor is usually also a person with reasons that can be understood.
intellectual_concerns: Slavery, coerced reproduction and the ownership of bodies, transposed into alien biology; race and the inheritance of racial power; symbiosis, dependency and the impossibility of a clean escape from the other; community, mutual obligation and the founding of a religion; climate collapse, scarcity and migration; and the ethics of survival, which is always someone else's cost.
historical_significance: Butler is the most influential Black American writer of speculative fiction and the one through whom the genre's engagement with race and power is dated into two periods. Kindred is taught as American literature rather than as genre fiction, the MacArthur Fellowship of 1995 was the first given to a science-fiction writer, and 'Bloodchild' - with its Hugo, Nebula and Locus awards - is the story most often used to show that the field's best work is about love and obligation rather than gadgets; her influence on the writers who followed, and on the political reading of science fiction after 2016, is acknowledged on every side.
